name: Tudor

revival_periods.note: First as Jacobethan country-house pastiche, then as the dominant suburban idiom of the English-speaking world between the wars — the most successfully commercialised revival in history, and the least structurally honest.

geography.hearth: The court and its circle in the Thames valley and Home Counties, radiating from royal works at Hampton Court, Richmond and Nonsuch

lineage.note: Direct and unbroken. Tudor is late Perpendicular working for laymen instead of the Church: the same masons' lodges, the same four-centred arch, the same panel tracery, redirected by the dissolution of the monasteries after 1536 from abbey to country house.
Below the level of the great house, Tudor is a timber-framing style. The carpentry tradition supplies the roofs and the whole vocabulary of the smaller Tudor house.

Transmission is real but confined to ornament. Italian craftsmen worked physically in England — Torrigiano on Henry VII's tomb from 1512, Giovanni da Maiano's terracotta emperor roundels at Hampton Court in 1521 — but they brought motifs, not the system that generated them. No Tudor building is proportioned classically.

description.short: The last Gothic style in England and the first secular one: red brick, four-centred arches, gatehouse courtyards and extravagant chimney stacks, with Renaissance ornament stuck on like jewellery to a suit of armour.
description.long:
Tudor is the architecture of a new dynasty with a shaky claim, a nobility forbidden to build seriously fortified houses, and — after 1536 — an enormous transfer of monastic land into private hands. All three conditions show. The castle's apparatus survives as costume: battlements you cannot fight from, gatehouses that frame an approach rather than block one, moats crossed by permanent bridges. What replaces defence is display, and the display medium is brick, which in early Tudor England was still expensive and fashionable enough to be worth patterning with burnt headers into diaper lozenges across an entire elevation. The great chimney stacks — clustered octagonal or spiral shafts with moulded caps, standing far taller than any draught requires — are the period's signature, and they exist because a chimney in 1520 announced that your house had private heated chambers rather than one communal fire.

Structurally nothing has changed since 1450. The four-centred arch, the hood mould with carved label stops, the mullioned window with cusped lights, the arch-braced roof: this is Perpendicular practice. What is new is the plan's slow rotation toward symmetry. The medieval hall with its off-centre screens entry persists at the heart of the house, but the gatehouse range in front of it begins to be composed as a face — a centred arch, an oriel above it, flanking turrets — and once the front elevation is being composed as an image, the logic that will eventually destroy the hall has been admitted. Italian ornament arrives on that same front, brought by craftsmen imported through diplomatic channels, and sits on it as pure surface: a terracotta roundel of a Roman emperor set into a diapered brick wall over a Gothic arch, with no attempt to reconcile the three.

What Tudor was reacting against is best described as insecurity itself. Henry VII's building programme, and Wolsey's after it, were arguments for legitimacy made in brick. The dissolution then supplied both the sites and the material — thousands of tons of dressed stone from wrecked abbeys went straight into gentry houses, and the recycling is often visible in the masonry.

To stand in a Tudor courtyard is to be enclosed by warm, slightly irregular brick, dark with the burnt headers of the diaper pattern, under a skyline that is deliberately busy: crenellated parapets, gables, cupolas, and everywhere the chimneys, which give a Tudor roofscape its unmistakable vertical restlessness. The windows are wide and low, divided into many small leaded lights, and the glass is uneven enough to move as you move. Indoors, the great hall is still the largest room, still cold at the low end, still entered through the screens; but off the dais end there is now a warren of private chambers with linenfold panelling and small windows, and the future of the English house is in those rooms rather than in the hall.

defining_characteristics: The four-centred (Tudor) arch struck from four centres, used for doorways, fireplaces and window heads, and almost always set within a rectangular label mould with carved spandrels
Red brick as the fashionable material, laid in English bond and patterned with vitrified headers into diaper lozenges; stone dressings at openings, quoins and copings
Tall clustered chimney shafts — octagonal, spiral or moulded — standing well above the roofline as a deliberate compositional element
The gatehouse-and-courtyard plan, with the entrance range composed as a symmetrical face while the plan behind it remains medieval
Mullioned windows of many small leaded lights, wide rather than tall, with transoms in taller openings and hood moulds above
The great hall retained with dais, screens passage and open or moulded-beam roof, entered off-centre
Non-defensive military apparatus: crenellated parapets, corner turrets, gatehouse towers and moats used for effect
diagnostic_tells: Four-centred arch under a square label mould with carved or moulded spandrels — the single most reliable Tudor signature
Diaper patterning in dark burnt headers across a red brick field; the pattern is structural bond, not applied render, and can be read on the wall's raking sunlight
Chimney stacks with individually moulded and spiralled shafts rising from a shared moulded base — a chimney treated as sculpture
An oriel window directly over the entrance arch, corbelled out on moulded stone brackets, marking the great chamber inside
No classical order anywhere used structurally; where Renaissance ornament appears it is a roundel, a putto or a shell set into a Gothic surface

distinguished_from.difference: Tudor composes a gatehouse front and hides a medieval plan behind it; Elizabethan composes the whole house as a symmetrical block, uses classical orders on a frontispiece, glazes vastly more of the wall, and puts the hall on the entrance axis. If the facade has superimposed orders and more glass than wall, it is Elizabethan.

Same construction, different client and different programme. Gothic proper is ecclesiastical and manorial with no interest in the frontal composition; Tudor is secular, courtly, brick rather than stone in the lowlands, and beginning — only beginning — to think of the elevation as a picture.

The revival's half-timbering is applied to a stud or masonry wall rather than framed; its arches are cut from a single stone or moulded in cement instead of struck from four centres in voussoirs; its chimneys are veneer over a flue block. The revival also mixes Tudor with Jacobean and Cotswold sources freely, which no Tudor building does.

proportional_system.governing_logic: No governing system in the classical sense. Setting-out is by the geometry of the four-centred arch (two small radii at the springing, two long radii to the apex) and by the mullion light as a repeating unit; the rest is composed by eye against a symmetry axis established at the gatehouse.
typical_ratios: Four-centred arch rise to span roughly 1:3 to 1:4 — much flatter than any earlier Gothic arch
Mullion light width 400-500 mm, in leaded quarries of roughly 100 x 150 mm; window width is a whole number of lights
Window opening proportion horizontal overall, typically 1:1.5 to 1:3 width to height per light but 2:1 to 4:1 wide overall
Storey heights nearly equal; no graduated diminution, which is what most clearly separates Tudor from Georgian at a glance
Chimney shaft height above ridge 1.5 to 3 times the stack's own width
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Irregular and additive except across the composed entrance range, where a centred arch, flanking turrets and an oriel establish a local three-part symmetry that does not extend around the corner. Windows are placed where rooms need them.

massing_affinities.note: The E-plan and half-H are the standard gentry answer: hall range with projecting wings and a porch making the middle stroke of the E.
The great Tudor house is a courtyard house — a base court for service and an inner court for the family, as at Hampton Court.
The smaller timber-framed Tudor house after the hall is floored over and a lobby-entry stack inserted.
Jettied timber street ranges in Tudor towns, though brick Tudor rarely takes this form.

constraints.statement: Depressed arches must be true four-centred arches in voussoirs with the rise between 1:3 and 1:4 of the span. A flattened ellipse, a segmental arch, or a moulded one-piece head is forbidden.

test.note: 1:4 to 1:3 rise:span. The requirement that the arch be a true four-centred arch in voussoirs (not a flattened ellipse, segmental arch or moulded head) stays prose -- no arch-form-shape variable exists.

constraints.statement: Classical orders may not be used structurally. Renaissance ornament is permitted only as inset panels, roundels or cresting on an otherwise Gothic surface, and may not exceed roughly 5 percent of the elevation.

test.note: Tests the 5 percent coverage ceiling. Where classical ornament may appear (inset panels, roundels, cresting only, never structural) stays prose.

constraints.statement: Windows are divided by stone or oak mullions into lights of 400-500 mm with leaded glazing; no sash windows and no single-pane openings. Where a window exceeds about 1.4 m in height it takes a transom.
Chimney stacks must rise at least 1.5 times their own width above the ridge and be moulded or shafted. A flush or clipped stack destroys the roofscape on which the style depends.

test.note: Chimney rise expressed in inches over its own width, both in inches, to test the stated 1.5x ratio. 'Moulded or shafted' stays prose.

constraints.statement: Battlements, turrets and moats are permitted as display only where the composition is clearly non-defensive; arrow loops, machicolation and portcullis grooves are forbidden as false archaeology.

exemplars.name: Hampton Court Palace, Base Court and Clock Court
exemplars.note: Begun 1515 for Cardinal Wolsey and taken by Henry VIII in 1529; Great Hall 1532-35. Diapered brick, gatehouse ranges, Maiano's terracotta roundels of 1521, and the definitive Tudor chimneyscape.

exemplars.name: Layer Marney Tower
exemplars.note: Built c.1520-25 for Henry, first Lord Marney. An eight-storey brick gatehouse with terracotta cresting and window dressings — a gatehouse so far outgrowing its house that the house was never finished.

exemplars.name: Compton Wynyates
exemplars.note: Built for Sir William Compton in the early sixteenth century, incorporating salvaged material. The least regularised of the great Tudor houses: a courtyard plan of astonishing picturesque irregularity in warm pink brick.

exemplars.name: Sutton Place
exemplars.note: Built 1521-33 for Sir Richard Weston. An early courtyard house, later opened on one side, whose terracotta ornament and near-symmetrical entrance front mark the first serious English negotiation with Renaissance detail.

sources: Maurice Howard, The Early Tudor Country House: Architecture and Politics 1490-1550 (1987)
John Summerson, Architecture in Britain 1530-1830 (9th ed., 1993)
Mark Girouard, Life in the English Country House (1978)
Nikolaus Pevsner et al., The Buildings of England (county volumes)
R. W. Brunskill, Brick Building in Britain (1990)

proportion_packs.note: tudor is named directly in timber-bay's applies_to, and the style's own lineage confirms why: it descends_from english-medieval-timber-frame at weight 0.6, and 'below the level of the great house, Tudor is a timber-framing style. The carpentry tradition supplies the roofs and the whole vocabulary of the smaller Tudor house.' No order pack is bound: c02 forbids classical orders being used structurally at all and caps applied Renaissance ornament at roughly 5 percent of the elevation as inset panels only, which is more restrictive than elizabethan and rules out even a cautious reference binding.

Judgment binding (not in applies_to). Scoped to the smaller, domestic-scale Tudor house — the hall-and-parlor type this style's own massing_affinities record as common 'after the hall is floored over and a lobby-entry stack inserted' — not to the courtyard great houses (Hampton Court, Compton Wynyates), whose halls and state rooms remain governed by the style's own figured ratios and lie well outside the pack's ordinary-room scale.

Secondary behind `timber-bay`. The panel figures apply, and one thing about this node should be read from `timber-bay` rather than here: its storey heights are 'nearly equal; no graduated diminution, which is what most clearly separates Tudor from Georgian at a glance'. That is a direct contradiction of `styles/german-fachwerk.json`'s storeys 'diminishing upward by roughly 10-15 percent' -- two half-timbering traditions doing opposite things with the same construction -- and it belongs to the frame pack rather than to the panel pack, which is why this one does not carry a diminution rule at all.
